title: Can young post-fire forests regulate microclimate? Insights from UAV LiDAR and electronic nose measurements
content:
Abstract
European forests are increasingly exposed to interacting natural disturbances, including prolonged drought, bark beetle outbreaks, windthrow, and large high-severity wildfires. These compound events often occur in close succession, reshaping forest structure, surface conditions, and near-ground microclimates. Although the immediate post-fire microclimate is well understood, a critical knowledge gap remains regarding when regenerating vegetation begins to regain the capacity to affect microclima. In this study, we examined whether early-stage post-fire vegetation exhibits any measurable ability to buffer microclimatic conditions. We combined high-resolution Unmanned Aerial Vehicle-based LiDAR data with microclimate measurements collected using an electronic nose. Structural metrics derived from normalized LiDAR point clouds were spatially linked with microclimate observations, and linear models were used to identify the vegetation attributes most strongly associated with near-ground temperature and humidity. Our results show that near-ground temperature is mostly shaped by altitude gradients in rugged terrain; however, early structural features already contribute detectable yet modest cooling effects. In flat areas, maximum vegetation height partially moderated temperature, while in steeper terrain, structural variability, and low-height vegetation cover provided the clearest cooling signal. These findings demonstrate that the first signs of microclimatic buffering re-emerge within 3 years after fire, but their strength depends strongly on topography and the developing stand structure.
